categories.label: Structural Mismatch Between Standard Payment Clauses and Offsite Production
categories.memo: Covers how CCDC and similar standard-form payment mechanisms, drafted around on-site measurement of completed work, fail to accommodate factory-based production, upfront financing needs, and off-site storage/transport, generating ambiguity and litigation.

codes.label: On-site measurement basis of progress payment clauses
codes.description: Standard payment clauses (e.g., CCDC 14 s.5.2.3) certify progress based on on-site inspection/completion, which is incompatible with modular/offsite production occurring largely in the factory.

codes.label: Ambiguous definition of 'Products' for prefabricated modules
codes.description: CCDC's definition of Products as materials/equipment 'incorporated into the work' creates uncertainty over whether fabricated but undelivered/uninstalled modules qualify for payment.

codes.label: Inability to claim for fabricated but undelivered/uninstalled modules
codes.description: Unfavorable payment terms preventing claims for modules manufactured but not yet delivered or incorporated create cash flow burdens for modular contractors, indicating a need for new contract terms recognizing off-site fabrication and storage stages.

codes.label: Shift from 'work done' to 'work due' compensation
codes.description: MMC payment mechanisms need to move away from compensating only physically completed on-site work toward recognizing offsite manufacturing progress and design/engineering work transferred to manufacturers.

codes.label: Unclear payment terms as litigation driver
codes.description: Court case analysis shows unclear payment terms are the leading cause of MOC-related litigation, more so than for conventional construction, reflecting the inadequacy of adapted standard contracts.

codes.label: Insurance coverage gaps for stored/in-transit modules
codes.description: Current risk allocation and insurance provisions do not adequately extend coverage to modules during transportation or storage outside the site and factory, compounding payment security risk.

categories.label: Upfront Financing and Cash Flow Risk in Offsite Delivery
categories.memo: Addresses the higher initial capital requirements of offsite/modular construction, financial fragility of suppliers/manufacturers, and the mismatch between conventional cash flow assumptions and MMC's front-loaded cost structure.

codes.label: Higher upfront capital costs of OSC/MiC
codes.description: Offsite/modular projects require significantly greater initial capital investment than conventional construction, particularly in early phases, threatening the financial stability of clients and contractors alike.

codes.label: Incompatibility of conventional cash flow systems with fragmented OSC supply chains
codes.description: Standard cash flow modelling assumes a relatively linear, on-site progression of work and does not account for the complex, fragmented, multi-party nature of modular supply chains.

codes.label: Owner/client payment delay risk
codes.description: Payment delays by clients are consistently identified as the most damaging factor to contractor and manufacturer cash flow, and are especially disruptive in OSC given high upfront material/manufacturing costs already incurred.

codes.label: Insolvency risk among specialist MMC suppliers
codes.description: The financial fragility of specialist offsite suppliers heightens concern about payment security, since their insolvency can disrupt project delivery and expose other parties to loss.

codes.label: Lack of contingency funds for scope changes
codes.description: Non-availability of spare funds for additional work is identified as a top financial dispute cause in OSC, since scope changes after manufacturing begins are costly and must be addressed through clear change-order and compensation provisions.

codes.label: Research gap on procurement approach and OSC cash flow
codes.description: The relationship between project delivery/procurement method selection and cash flow performance in non-conventional (OSC/MiC) projects remains understudied, limiting evidence-based contract drafting.

categories.label: Dynamic Compensation and Incentive Mechanisms for Schedule Coordination
categories.memo: Covers proposed alternatives to fixed/static payment terms that dynamically price the cost impact of delivery date changes between factories/suppliers and contractors, aiming to align incentives given their separate for-profit status.

codes.label: Fixed compensation places all schedule-change risk on the supplier
codes.description: Traditional just-in-time delivery compensation is static and requires suppliers/factories to absorb all costs of contractor-driven schedule changes, regardless of magnitude or direction.

codes.label: Contracts as rigid 'push' mechanisms during variations
codes.description: Rather than enabling flexible pull-based coordination, existing contracts force rigid compliance when schedule variations occur, causing each party to manage disruptions unilaterally instead of collaboratively.

codes.label: Dynamic surcharge/incentive compensation tied to real-time cost impact
codes.description: A quantitative compensation mechanism that assigns surcharges for unfavourable delivery changes and incentives/rebates for favourable ones better reflects actual cost impact than fixed contractual payment terms.

codes.label: Supplier rebate for honoring original delivery schedule
codes.description: A contractual rebate is granted to the contractor only if the originally agreed delivery date is honored, discouraging opportunistic rescheduling and aligning incentives across the supply chain.

codes.label: Schedule float as a tradable contractual resource
codes.description: Contractors' float time can be strategically offered to factories in exchange for financial incentives, turning schedule flexibility itself into a negotiable contractual asset, bounded by precedence constraints and contractual maximum-change allowances.

codes.label: Absence of penalties for contractor-driven schedule changes
codes.description: Under standard blanket/master agreements, contractors face no penalty for altering delivery dates after order placement, encouraging opportunistic behavior that imposes inventory and financing costs on suppliers.

codes.label: Contracts as binding fallback absent negotiated coordination
codes.description: Even where dynamic coordination mechanisms are proposed, original contractual terms remain the binding default when parties cannot reach a mutually beneficial adjustment.

codes.label: Quality-price supplier selection with delivery obligations
codes.description: Selecting suppliers on a quality-price basis rather than lowest tender, combined with contractual delivery obligations, has supported successful JIT coordination in public sector projects.

categories.label: Revenue-Sharing and Multi-Party Profit Coordination Contracts
categories.memo: Covers contractual mechanisms distributing subsidies, revenue, and profit between developers/contractors/suppliers to align incentives for prefabrication uptake, going beyond simple fixed-price arrangements.

codes.label: Revenue-sharing to pass through government subsidies
codes.description: Developers can use revenue-sharing contract mechanisms to transfer government subsidies to general contractors, incentivizing higher prefabrication levels.

codes.label: Limits of simple revenue-sharing contracts
codes.description: A basic revenue-sharing contract, even set at its coordinating optimum, fails to achieve genuine mutual benefit, often favoring the contractor due to information asymmetry over cost data.

codes.label: Combined fixed-transfer-payment and revenue-sharing contracts
codes.description: A more sophisticated contract combining a fixed transfer payment with variable revenue sharing can achieve genuine Pareto-improving coordination between developer and contractor.

codes.label: Environmental responsibility cost-sharing mechanisms
codes.description: Reward-penalty and subsidy policy mechanisms shape how environmental responsibility costs and burdens are allocated contractually between contractor and supplier, with implications for profitability and coordination.

categories.label: Inventory, Warehousing, and Logistics Cost Allocation
categories.memo: Covers financial burdens created by mismatched delivery and assembly schedules, including third-party storage costs and idle inventory, and how contracts do or do not allocate these costs.

codes.label: Limited on-site storage capacity forcing third-party warehousing costs
codes.description: General contractors' limited on-site inventory capacity for offsite components forces reliance on costly external warehousing when assembly schedules lag behind delivery.

codes.label: Idle inventory waste from delivery-assembly schedule mismatch
codes.description: A significant share of delivered offsite components sit unused in on-site warehouses for extended periods, representing quantifiable non-value-added cost that current payment/scheduling contracts do not address.

codes.label: Inventory cost burden shifted to fabricator under rigid contracts
codes.description: Contractor-driven rescheduling under standard master agreements imposes inventory, storage, financing, and insurance costs on the fabricator, revealing a risk-allocation failure that inflates costs for the whole supply chain.

codes.label: Information platforms enabling coordinated cost visibility
codes.description: Shared information/IT platforms are needed to give real-time visibility of production and inventory status, supporting contractual mechanisms to coordinate delivery changes between financially independent parties.

categories.label: Automated and Technology-Enabled Payment Processing
categories.memo: Covers blockchain/smart-contract-based automation of progress payments in modular construction as an alternative to manual, third-party-administered payment certification, distinguished here by its cash-flow/administrative function rather than technical mechanics (see T5).

codes.label: Blockchain-automated progress payment frameworks
codes.description: Blockchain and smart contracts can automate progress payment administration in MiC projects via staged frameworks (preparation, initialization, execution), reducing reliance on third-party administrators.

codes.label: Reduced reliance on third-party payment administrators
codes.description: Traditional contractual payment enforcement depends on costly third parties (administrators, lawyers); blockchain-enabled automation can reduce this cost and associated dispute potential.

codes.label: Partial automation limitations of current systems
codes.description: Existing BIM-blockchain payment systems require manual data updates, address only single delivery systems, and do not account for disputes, limiting their applicability to complex modular payment structures.

codes.label: Extension of automated payment logic to post-completion obligations
codes.description: Smart contract payment logic can be extended beyond progress payments to manage defects liability period obligations, broadening the scope of automated cash flow management.

categories.label: Procurement/Delivery Method Selection and Payment Structure Fit
categories.memo: Covers how the choice of delivery method and contract form (D&B, two-stage, standard forms) interacts with payment structuring needs specific to MMC/offsite construction.

codes.label: Design-Build favored for consolidating payment and design responsibility
codes.description: D&B contracts are favored in MMC because they consolidate design and construction into a single contractual unit, easing coordination of payment against offsite manufacturing progress.

codes.label: Two-stage procurement balancing cost certainty and client risk aversion
codes.description: Two-stage procurement approaches are preferred by clients to defer full commitment while still gaining OSC benefits, affecting when and how payment terms are finalized.

codes.label: Removal/reduction of retention and liquidated damages
codes.description: Common bespoke amendments in MMC contracts target reducing or removing retention and liquidated damages provisions, reflecting suppliers' need for more predictable cash flow given upfront manufacturing costs.

codes.label: No dedicated standard contracts for MOC in Canada
codes.description: Absence of MOC-specific standard contracts forces adaptation of conventional construction contracts (e.g., CCDC 2, CCDC 14), which do not adequately address offsite payment/cash flow needs and correlates with higher litigation risk.

codes.label: Reuse of unmodified contract templates
codes.description: Recycling standard contract templates from prior projects without adequate modification for offsite payment needs is identified as a major source of ambiguity and dispute risk.
